headline: A virus-scan reply that never says FOUND no longer stalls the scanner
summary: `b.mail.scan`'s ClamAV client read the threat name out of the daemon's reply with a pattern that could be made to take exponential time, and the reply is accepted up to 50 MiB. It reads the name in one pass now. The check that should have caught it read regex literals only and drove them with subjects of one repeated character, so the pattern never reached its costly branch under it. Widening that check is what found this.

items.title: `b.mail.scan` reads a ClamAV reply in one pass
items.body:
The ClamAV INSTREAM client took the threat name out of `stream: <name> FOUND` with a lazy run between two whitespace quantifiers. A space matches both of them, so on a reply that never says FOUND the engine tries every way of dividing one run of spaces between the two before the match fails. A reply with 2,400 spaces cost 1.8 seconds, and one with 8,192 did not finish within five.

The daemon sends that reply, and it is accepted up to `maxResponseBytes`, which is 50 MiB on the strict profile. So whatever is on the other end of the socket sets the size of that search, whether that is a compromised scanner, something in the path of an unencrypted connection to it, or a reply shaped by the file being scanned.

The reader takes the name in one pass now, and returns the same name the pattern did on every reply shape. Whitespace is the set JavaScript matches rather than the ASCII part of it, so a name wrapped in a non-breaking space is still a name. A name never spans a line, though the spaces around it may, so a label whose spaces cross a line names something on the next one. When a label and the verdict token are separated by nothing but spaces, the name is taken from those spaces, and a threat named `FOUND` is read as the name rather than as the verdict. A reply carrying a clean line and an infected one is read from the infected one, so an infection cannot be downgraded to clean. A check compares the reader against the pattern it replaced across 27,335 reply shapes, which is every sequence of up to seven of the pieces a reply is made of.

There is nothing to do on upgrade. Verdicts, threat names and audit records are unchanged.

items.title: Three credential and command readers no longer slow on a run of spaces
items.body:
The widened check found the same shape in three more places, all reading attacker-supplied text: the `Bearer` credential in `b.middleware.scimServer`, the same credential in `b.middleware.attachUser`, and the arguments of an IMAP `NOTIFY SET` command in `b.mail.server`.

Each spelled the value it wanted as `(.+)` after `\s+`. Both accept a space, so text made of the scheme or command and a long run of spaces can be divided between them at every space, and the engine tries every division before the match fails. Measured on each: about 5ms at 4,096 characters and between 72ms and 78ms at 16,384, which is four times the input for fifteen times the work.

All three now require the value to start at a character that is not a space, which is the only division there is. At 16,384 characters they take under a millisecond. What they read is unchanged for every value that is not made entirely of spaces; one that is reads as absent rather than as a value made of spaces, so `scimServer` answers a header of `Bearer` and nothing but spaces with the same `Missing Bearer token` it gives a header with no credential at all, rather than passing a string of spaces to the token callback.

The `scimServer` header is already refused above 8 KiB before the pattern runs, which bounds what that one could cost. The `attachUser` reader is the one the check cannot see, since its pattern is built from the scheme rather than written out, and it carries a test of its own.

There is nothing to do on upgrade.

items.title: `b.mtlsCa.parseGeneration` reads a subject DN in one pass
items.body:
The widened check found a second pattern. `parseGeneration` read the `OU=CAv{N}` generation tag out of a certificate's subject with `(?:^|[\r\n]|(?<!\\)[,+])\s*OU=CAv(\d+)`. A newline is both an RDN separator and whitespace, so on text where separators and spaces run together, every separator is a start position and the `\s*` after it scans the rest of the run before failing: 8,192 characters cost 22ms and 32,768 cost 365ms.

A certificate does not deliver that text today. Node renders a subject as one `type=value` per line and escapes a newline inside a value as `\0A`, so the character after a separator is the next attribute type and the `\s*` matches nothing. The reading no longer rests on that escaping: the DN is split on its separators and each field is read from its own start, once. At 32,768 characters it takes 0.14ms.

What it reports is unchanged, including the two cases the lookbehind was there for: an escaped `\,` or `\+` inside a value does not separate, and a multi-valued RDN joined with `+` does. The reader was compared against the pattern it replaced on 299,611 subject shapes.

There is nothing to do on upgrade.

items.title: Vendored PKI bundle moves to 0.6.39
items.body:
`lib/vendor/blamejs-pki.cjs` carries `@blamejs/pki` 0.6.39, up from the 0.6.30 that shipped in 0.19.2. This is shipped code: `b.mtlsCa` and `b.auth.passkey` run it.

Three of the versions bind an enrollment to the connection it is sent on. 0.6.31 reports the RFC 5929 `tls-unique` value of a TLS 1.2 connection and accepts a request body built from it, per RFC 7030 section 3.5. 0.6.32 lets `simpleenroll` and `simplereenroll` take a CSR builder, so the CSR is signed over the `tls-unique` of the connection that carries it rather than of an earlier one. 0.6.33 adds the RFC 9266 `tls-exporter` binding for TLS 1.3, 32 bytes under the label `EXPORTER-Channel-Binding`; it is withheld below TLS 1.3, where RFC 9266 section 2 also requires the RFC 7627 extended master secret that Node gives no way to confirm.

The rest refuse things they used to accept. 0.6.34 reports an injected transport that does not return a promise as a typed option error naming the option, in every client that takes one. 0.6.35 through 0.6.37 refuse a natively signed C509 certificate that spells an extension, an algorithm or a value in a redundant form instead of the registry entry naming the same thing, so a certificate has one encoding and an issuer signature cannot cover two different C509 byte strings. 0.6.38 lets a trust anchor name the namespace its root is trusted for, and `pki.path.validate` enforces that as the initial name-constraint state. 0.6.39 builds a verdict with its fields rather than writing them on afterward, so a value left on `Object.prototype` cannot answer a question the verification never asked.

There are no API changes and nothing to do on upgrade. The bundle ships with no dependencies and no install hooks, and its recorded SHA-256 is checked against the file on every build.

items.title: The lexer identifies which text is a pattern
items.body:
The check found patterns by matching slashes across a line. Whether a `/` opens a pattern or divides two numbers or sits inside a string is a lexing question, and answering it with a search over the line got it wrong in both directions: 2,684 spans that are comment prose, URL paths inside strings and `/* */` openers were measured as patterns, while 5 real ones were missed.

The embedded WebAuthn attestation roots are where that showed. A base64 line of a certificate contains slashes, and the text between two of them parses as a pattern whose two `+` quantifiers measure superlinear once a probe reaches them, so the check was on course to report a certificate as a slow regular expression.

The framework already contains a lexer, and the comment rule already shares its classifier with the tool that sweeps comments. The linear-time check now uses that lexer, and reads the 893 pattern literals `lib/` actually holds, 608 of them distinct.

A lexer emits a template literal as one token, so a pattern written inside a substitution sits within that token and reaches nothing reading pattern tokens. The code between `${` and its matching brace is read in turn, to any depth, and the offsets are carried through so a report still points at the line the pattern is on. Where a substitution ends is found by counting its braces, which reads an opening brace written inside a character class as structural. Whether a `${` is escaped is decided by whether the run of backslashes before it is odd, since `\\${` opens a substitution while `\${` does not.

Lexer corrections came with it, all of the same shape: a statement may begin with a pattern, and the tokenizer read the slash that starts one as division. That happens after the `)` of a control-flow header, and after `else` and `do`, each of which governs a statement that need not be braced. A `}` that closed an object closed an expression, so the slash after it divides, while one that closed a block ended a statement; which a brace is cannot be read off the brace, so it is decided at the matching `{` by the classifier the comment stripper in the same file already used, two answers to one structural question having drifted apart. What that classifier is told about a preceding colon matters too: a colon separating a property from its value or closing a ternary is followed by a value, while one ending a label or a `case` is followed by a statement, and `label: {}` opens a block. So does a keyword that forbids a line terminator after it once one appears: `yield` on its own line has ended its statement, and the brace below opens a block rather than the object it would otherwise yield. A postfix `++` or `--` ends an expression, so the slash after it divides; reading it as a pattern opener swallowed the rest of the line and took the opening slash of the next real pattern with it. Which form it is depends on whether there was something to operate on, whether a line terminator came between, since one ends the statement and leaves the operator to start the next, and whether the paren before it closed a control-flow header rather than an expression. A prefix one is followed by its operand, which may itself begin with a pattern. A line comment ends at every line terminator and not only at a newline, and the two Unicode ones are whitespace like the rest: a lexer that skips them as unknown leaves no gap between the statements they separate, and one that reads past them swallows the rest of the file as a comment. `break` and `continue` take a label and nothing else, and nothing divides a label, so a slash after either the keyword or the label it carries opens a pattern; with the semicolon left to insertion, the pattern on the next line is the next statement, and reading that slash as division emitted no pattern token for it at all. The header case is now decided at the matching `(`, which is where the comment stripper beside it already decided the same question. It reads through the transparent word in `for await (`, and a control keyword used as a property name does not open a header, since `obj.if(x) / 2` divides. The lexer now also reads the `v` flag, which it stopped before, leaving the flag to be read as a name and the pattern rebuilt without it. That flag enables character classes that nest, which this reader does not parse, so a pattern using it is reported unmeasured with that reason rather than measured under a shape that might not be the one that runs. The framework has no such pattern today.

items.title: Composed patterns are measured for linear time
items.body:
The linear-time check extracts regex literals from the source. A pattern built with `new RegExp("...")`, or through a helper that wraps one, is not a literal, so 33 of them went unmeasured. That included every entry in the table `b.guardSql` matches statements against, which is the one place in the framework a regex is pointed at hostile SQL by design.

Both shapes are reconstructed and measured now: a direct `new RegExp` on a string, and a one-argument helper that wraps `new RegExp` with fixed flags. A pattern assembled from a variable or a `join()` cannot be rebuilt without running the file, and is still left to the module's own tests.

All 33 measure linear. Four of them are refused by `b.guardRegex.assertSafe`, which is the framework's own conservative screen; they now carry a measurement rather than an assertion.

items.title: The text a pattern reached by is preserved as written
items.body:
Two ways of reading a pattern lost part of it before it was measured.

A group offering a choice was read by taking one branch. Which branch a pattern can actually take is not always decidable from the text before it: an assertion inside a branch can read what precedes it, what follows it, or the quantified body the reading stops short of, and three ways of deciding it each got a different shape wrong. So the choice is no longer made. Every branch is read, and the probe drives all of them. The branch that reaches the body drives it, and the ones that cannot fail at once.

A pattern given to the constructor as a string is re-spelled as a literal so pattern and flags can be told apart. Every slash in it was escaped, including one the pattern had already escaped. `new RegExp("^(?:\\/|/)+$")` became a pattern matching a backslash and a slash on one side and a slash on the other, so two alternatives that were the same alternative stopped being the same, and a pattern that backtracks exponentially read as fast. A slash the pattern escapes is left as it is, and one inside a character class is left alone too, since a literal does not escape it there.

items.title: A pattern is driven past its opening literal
items.body:
Subjects were built from one character repeated. A pattern that opens with a literal fails at that token on such a subject and never reaches what follows it, so a costly body behind `\bCOPY\b` was never reached and read as fast. The prefix a pattern requires is now read off it verbatim, punctuation included, and seeded into subjects of its own. Where a pattern requires several literals in order, the runs joined in order are seeded too. A subject carrying one of them stops at the next.

The filler is drawn from the pattern itself. `a` and a space do not enter a body that accepts only `x`, and some ambiguity needs a motif rather than a character: `(?:ab|ab)+$` costs on `ab` repeated and returns at once on either letter alone. Each subject is also tried with a trailing character the pattern cannot accept. A pattern only backtracks on its way to failing.

The characters a repetition consumes are chosen before the rest. The filler list is capped and filled in order, so a long prefix used to spend it: `^PREFIX(z+)+$` got `a`, a space, and four letters of its prefix and never `z`, so every subject failed at the prefix and the body behind it was never entered.

Which character a token accepts is asked of the engine rather than read off the token's own letters. `\d` names a set that the letter `d` is not in, and `\x7a` is the character `z`, so a filler taken from the text enters neither. An escape is read as one token for the same reason: split into `\x`, `7` and `a` it yields two characters the pattern refuses. A negated class is entered by a character it does not list, which is found the same way.

Where a token names a SET, a member of it is chosen rather than the reading stopping there. That is one rule covering what were four separate holes. An escape names a character, so `^\x50REFIX(z+)+$` requires `PREFIX` and not `xREFIX`. A class still requires one character, so `^[A-F]PREFIX(z+)+$` requires `APREFIX` rather than nothing at all. A group that carries no quantifier is required too, so `^(?:A|A)PREFIX(z+)+$` requires `APREFIX` where the reading used to stop at the parenthesis; a lookaround is the exception, since it matches without taking anything, and `^(?!X)...` requires no `X` at all. A motif is what a quantified group repeats and need not be a word, so `(?:a-|a-)+$` is driven with `a-`, which it costs on, rather than with either character alone, which it returns at once on. And a class inside a motif is a set too, so `(?:a\d|a\d)+$` is driven with `a0`. In each case the old reading stopped at the token, no subject satisfied the anchor, and the body behind it was entered by nothing.

A seed comes from what a pattern MATCHES rather than from how it is spelled: backslashes used to be stripped, which made `u03A9` a word of `[Ω]` and `bCOPY` one of `\bCOPY`, and a subject starting with either fails the anchor. The empty string is always among the seeds, tried after the specific ones. It is the whole subject for a pattern with no literal in it, and it is the only subject that reaches a body behind an alternative the prefix did not take, as in `^(?:X|(?:,-|,-)+)$`. A class is answered by a member of itself, read off the class, so `(?:[q]|[q])+$` is driven with `q` and `(?:[Ω]|[Ω])+$` with the character it names, whatever its codepoint; a motif is bounded by what a subject can carry rather than by a short fixed length, so `(?:abcdefg|abcdefg)+$` is driven with the seven characters it costs on; `\cA` is control-A rather than the letter `c`; a pattern with no literal in it at all, like `^(?:,-|,-)+$`, is driven with its motif alone, where before the motif was derived and then never used; and a group nested inside an alternative contributes the string it matches, so `(?:a(?:b|b)|a(?:b|b))+$` is driven with `ab`, its alternation divided at the group's own bar rather than at every bar in it; a fixed quantifier keeps an alternative fixed-length, so `(?:ab{2}|ab{2})+$` is driven with `abb`; and a fixed quantifier in a required prefix repeats what it follows, so `^A{2}PREFIX(z+)+$` requires `AAPREFIX`; and a Unicode property escape is one token naming a set, read under the flag that makes it one, so `(?:\p{Letter}0|\p{Letter}0)+$` is driven with a letter and a zero rather than with the letters of the word `Letter`. A set whose members lie outside any range worth walking is searched for rather than looked up in a list of scripts someone thought to write down, so `\p{Script=Adlam}` is answered too.

The pieces a subject is built from are assembled by one function now. Thirty-five patterns of these shapes are driven through it and each is asserted to be given a character its body repeats, twenty-five pin the prefix a pattern requires, four pin that no seed is built from a pattern's spelling, and the claim underneath them is checked over 312 generated shapes: the prefix a pattern requires is a string that pattern accepts, and one that does not already match it.

Where a group offers a choice, every branch of it is read rather than the first one that spells a literal, and every such group is read rather than only the first. Which branch a pattern can take is not always decidable from the text before it, since an assertion inside one can read what precedes it, what follows it, or the quantified body the reading stops short of. So the choice is not made: each branch becomes a subject of its own, the one that reaches the body drives it, and the ones that cannot fail at once. Reading only the first group's first four branches left two families measured by nothing, each found by moving the branch that reaches the body through every position: a fifth branch was never built, and a group after the first was never varied, which left `^A(?:x|x)L(?:P(?!z)|Q(?=z))(z+)+$` reading as fast although it takes 892ms on `AxLQ`. One group varies per reading, since enumerating combinations across groups is exponential; the bounds are four groups and twelve branches, against the 597 patterns `lib/` holds, of which 518 offer no choice at all, the most any offers is three groups, and the widest offers twelve branches.

And the whole of it is checked end to end. Twenty-nine patterns that are catastrophic are each driven with the subjects their own pieces build, and each has to measure as costly. Every gap listed above was invisible to a check on the pieces and visible to that one.

That is what found the ClamAV defect above. Reading the prefix as words joined by spaces was not enough on its own: `stream:` keeps its colon only when the prefix is taken verbatim.

items.title: An exemption marker is checked wherever it is written
items.body:
A marker that exempts a line from a rule was validated in `lib/` and `test/` only. Everywhere else the name went unchecked. Five markers had been sitting outside that scope, all naming a class that was renamed so that every use would be re-examined; the rename reached the markers the check could see and left these. None of them exempted anything: the rule they named reads the framework's own source, not those files. They are removed.

The check now reads scripts and the example apps too, skipping installed dependencies and build output. The example app runs a gate of its own with its own classes, so a marker under `examples/` is answered against that registry rather than the framework's; a name in neither is still reported.

items.title: A rule's advertised exemption is the one it honors
items.body:
Each rule carries a header naming the marker that exempts a site. That header is what a reader follows when the build stops on the rule. Ten named a class that had been renamed, so following one produced a marker the repository does not accept. Two more named a class that is registered while the rule never consults it, so the marker was accepted and had no effect, and the build failed again with the message the contributor had just tried to answer.

The ten now name the class they filter on. The two rules take no marker at all, and their headers now state that; their classes are retired, so writing one fails the build rather than being ignored. Eight more rules that never took a marker now state that on the line, which keeps their name and keeps the claim checkable.

A new check holds all of it, and asks the question per rule rather than across the file: a rule may not advertise a retired class, nor a registered class it does not consult, nor a class that is neither registered nor consulted anywhere. The last of these names an exemption no contributor can use.
